In a land a long, long time ago, Team Fortress 2 would be a critically acclaimed first person shooter. Boasting its colorful characters against the dreary palette of the Badlands, this game offered to many a wonderful experience. Later updates would add cosmetics, weapons, and a ton of other things to sink your teeth into. Some of those updates are not as well viewed by the community as others, like the addition of crazier and crazier hats. In recent years, the community has felt somewhat negatively towards the team of developers and their updates for this game. Though, there is something important to remember...

We first saw those deranged mercenaries nearly a decade ago! This game has been alive and kicking for a long time, and I doubt that you will soon see a day where these mercs aren't defying laws of physics, common sense, and sometimes all laws in general. You won't find many other games with a soviet in love with a 300 pound minigun that he just lugs around like it's nothing. Nor will you find a quick-witted, caffeine-fueled Bostonian who dances around the battlefield, dodging rockets and bullets like a madman. This game is very outlandish, and incredibly enjoyable. Even after years and years of pushing a payload down a track to blow up the enemies... people want to come back, because although there's some basis and objectives for the game modes, you never play the same game twice. Every match is a total surprise. Even competitively, the 9 classes and variety in what you can play with, it will give you a new experience nearly every time you play. 

Years of pushing a cart filled to the brim with explosives is a hard task. Thankfully, there are new faces, hats to wear, weapons to try, and a new experience to be had every single day..

TF2 is one of the best games ever made, but thanks to Valve's abhorrent neglect, I can no longer recommend this game to anyone.
 
TF2 has remained in a borderline unplayable state for over 5 years. Valve's official game servers are flooded with cheaters and cheating bots, rendering the game unplayable for most hours of the day. Players are now completely reliant on operating their own servers in order to enjoy the game. Valve has completely ignored TF2's problems, while simultaneously profiting millions off of in-game microtransactions year after year.

This neglectful treatment has clearly become a company-wide problem. Counter-Strike 2 is experiencing a cheater infestation. Left for Dead servers experience waves of DDOS attacks. And rather than maintain their currently offered and HEAVILY monetized titles, Valve has the audacity to be working on yet another game, guaranteed to be filled to the brim with monetization features, while leaving their other games to rot. It's nothing but pure greed from a multi-billion dollar corporation.

Rather than addressing the cheating bots, Valve has only opted to apply band-aid fixes in the form of removing in-game communication features for free to play accounts. Bot hosters frequently use in-game text and voice chat to spam nonsense, or even doxx other players. Given that these stopgaps are avoided by simply spending a few dollars on the in-game store, or by using stolen accounts, this has done nothing to mitigate the bot problem, and has only served to further punish players. This is all the effort Valve was willing to muster a few years ago, which only amplified the already horrific experiences for anyone new to the game.

It's laughable that Valve, with their vast resources, has allowed for these problems to persist as long as they have while doing absolutely nothing. Shameful. Pathetic. Asinine. No combination of words is enough to fully convey the weight of their willful neglect.

So long as TF2 is offered as playable with incentivized microtransactions, and Valve profits from it, it should at the very least be playable. Until it is, I can't recommend this game to anyone.

This isn't a joke review, I know I have close to 4k hours in this game and that's not including all the different mods/console versions I've played as I really, really, really love this game. It's been a staple of my teenage/young adult life, and there truly has never been nor will there ever be a game to replace it. I'm not recommending it because this game just isn't like it used to be due to neglect from its developers and the experience for a newer player is most likely to be abysmal. 

The game is infested with bots and cheaters as Valve, the multibillion dollar corporation with all the resources in the world, chooses to do nothing about it. Their way of "combating" this was butchering the experience for a free to play user by heavily restricting communication, instead of, you know, developing an anti-cheat that's actually worth a damn. 

But even then, I wouldn't mind cheaters that much if it weren't for the god-awful matchmaking system that's been stinking up this game since 2016 like a half-opened jar of rancid horse radish you forgot in the back of your cupboard since Bill Clinton's daughter got her dad's dick wet. Seriously, after all these years, I still cannot fathom a single positive thing it added to the game and we're reaping the consequences of it's addition as the bot/cheater problem wouldn't be anywhere near as bad as it is now if it weren't for it's inclusion. 

Even if you do get in a game that's absent of cheaters, there's still a good 80% chance that the game you join will be a complete steam roll either with or against your favor. Playing with friends and trying to introduce them to this game always goes south as it consists of: wait 10 minutes to be put in a match, wait another minute for everyone to join, have both rounds end in less than 5 minutes due to the teams being utterly stacked, wait 5 minutes for a map vote, then leave the game and re-queue for an additional 10 minutes anyways because half the server rage-quitted after last match. Oh, and pray to god one of your friends doesn't get autobalanced halfway through, as there's basically no way you can change teams unlike years before.

Because how you played the game before, you looked in the server browser, found a server that was running a map/gamemode you liked, joined with your friends, and if the game was unbalanced you could either manually join the losing team to help them, or have autoscramble kick in which worked at least half of the time. It wasn't perfect, but I 1000% prefer it over the utter nightmare that is modern matchmaking. It's not nostalgia either, a community made mod called Team Fortress 2 Classic has that old system I just mentioned and I can play that game for literal hours in a single day, something I haven't done with normal TF2 in the longest time due to how frustrating it is to simply get put in a match. I can't even really put my finger on it but this matchmaking system has been the WORST thing I have ever seen added to a video game and I think it's going to pre-maturely kill this game.

I have a bit of a love/hate relationship with this game's community, but at the end of the day I've realized if you play this in 2023 you're just going to encounter every flavor of manchild there is. Hope you enjoy playing with obnoxious furries, weaboos, racists, and pride flag waving weirdos you probably shouldn't have around your children. I guess there's nothing inherently wrong with having these people present in your playerbase, but if these groups consist of the majority, then that really says a lot about the absolute state of your game. 

We get "updates" every summer/Halloween/Christmas that consist of community made content with absolutely ZERO (0) quality control. I know the art style has been dead since the inclusion of paints in like 2010, but oh my god the new stuff that's being added to the game is almost inexcusable and quite embarrassing. I'm talking about cosmetics that have no regard for the intended art-style and throw team/class recognition out the window, maps that not only play like shit but look like baby's first project with the hammer editor being OFFICIALLY ADDED TO THE GAME. Valve literally cannot be damned to get at least 1 single person to check the quality of the content that's being included to one of their most popular IPs that rakes in tons of cash. 

So yeah, if you're a new player or somebody thinking about getting back into TF2, I wouldn't bother. I want this game to be remembered for it's stunning legacy throughout the early '10s, offering the most fun experience you could have online, and not the pathetic zombie that it is now. There's nothing like it, but there's a lot of video games out there you can waste your time with. Don't waste your time with this one. Save it for something more enjoyable and do not enable Valve's neglect by blowing your wallet on stupid cosmetic items.

Team Fortress 2 is, in a nutshell, a team-based FPS in which the Red and Blue team compete against each other with 9 different classes in various game modes.

PROS:
+ Free to play 
+ Many maps, gamemodes and tons and tons of weaponry and cosmetics, both official and community-made
+ Very beginner-friendly. Unlike games like CS:GO, new players have a very fair chance of beating even experienced players
+ You will get weekly drops of weapons (sometimes cosmetics too)
+ A huge interest in trading items via a network of trading servers and sites. Skilled traders can make profit in the form of real money as well
+ Tons of alternate gamemode servers like x10, randomizer, medieval, deathruns, surfing, jumping, trading, tons of workshop maps, etc.  
+ It depends if you consider this as a pro, but there's explosivejumping. It's so incredibly fun and there's over 500 downloadable jumpmaps and an active community behind it. At least a fifth of my hours in this game are spent on explosivejumping
+ TF2 uses the Source engine, a very comfortable engine and very easy to configure and save settings with 
+ Trading cards 

CONS: 
- The community can be kind of toxic and/or cringy at times
- Valve keeps adding more and more updates people generally don't enjoy 
- If you play TF2 now, you'll play with a lot of weapons that used to be different (usually better) in the past. Occasionally weapons get re-balanced and often break because of it

There's a reason this game still has a player base [i]almost 20 years later[/i]. Nine classes that all play completely different from each other, which sounds basic but most shooters still can't get that right. Every class has a real identity to it, and the way they play off each other is what makes the game work. You actually have to think about what your team needs.

The community does more for this game than Valve does at this point. Custom maps, community items, seasonal events, all of that. Valve barely touches it anymore but people still show up every day and it still feels fun, which says a lot about how solid the core gameplay is.

MvM deserves its own mention. The co-op community used to be pretty rough on new players but it's gotten a lot better over time. There's plenty of guides on YouTube and other places if you want to go in prepared, but honestly most people are way more patient now than they used to be. If you ever need someone to run with, feel free to add me.

It's not without its issues though. Bots aren't as bad as they used to be thankfully, but you'll still run into the occasional hacker. Matchmaking can be rough, and some of the older mechanics show their age. But when you're in a good match with people actually playing their roles, nothing else feels like it. TF2 has this energy that other team shooters try to capture but can't quite nail.

It's free. If you like shooters at all, just try it.

"Team Fortress 2" is a timeless multiplayer game that has managed to stay relevant for years despite being released in 2007. Its unique blend of humor, class-based gameplay, and strategic depth has created a dedicated community that still enjoys the game today. The colorful, cartoony art style and witty writing make it stand out in a sea of more serious first-person shooters. So many community servers now were not only struggling, but had straight up died to the point where only a few had remained and were constantly full cause no one had anywhere else to go. The bot crises I'd argue [i]is[/i], in fact, a direct result of the casual matchmaking system allowing bot hosters to fill party queues with them, (it only takes 4 full parties to fill a valve server btw). Team Fortress 2 is one of my favorite games and hat simulators of all time. It's not really much of a secret, given how many hours I've gotten in it plus the fact I've been playing it for over 10 years (although it was a while before I had a computer that could run it very well). It is more than just a game; it is a whole experience.

The gameplay is very addictive. The gunplay and counters feel just right, and no two classes play the same (which can't be said for some modern hero shooters). Team Fortress 2 showed that you only needed 9 classes maximum, instead of 20 or so. There are crates and microtransactions sure, but they aren't exactly forced upon you; you can simply get free item drops by just playing the game on servers (at least if they are secure VAC-enabled ones). A lot of the maps are very memorable; 2Fort, Dustbowl, Badwater etc. and a dozen of community created maps that would be too much to list here. Even with (non-cheating) singleplayer bots, the game is still very fun.

Personality and style wise, TF2 had the best a shooter game could ever have. The classes are all fun to witness, and even 17 years later they still feel irreplaceable, with perfect voice acting and beyond memorable and hilarious dialog. It's not like some other games where they are just generic, too. Each class was designed with shapes and silhouettes in mind, creating easily identifiable looks (i.e. if someone is outlined behind a wall, you could tell which class it is even from afar). The art-style of the game, inspired by J.C. Leyendecker, really made it timeless, and it still looks good to this day; an incredible feat for a game from 2007, a time when most games went for a muddy realistic look (a large portion of which haven't aged well visually). TF2 went for a heavily researched mixture of being cartoony and grounded, and it worked very, VERY well. It's not like some modern cartoony shooters that don't have reason behind the style, because this one does. There is also a story that is not forced upon you, being told through item descriptions, map objects, comics and shorts. It is wacky and adds a lot more to the game's world.

Now sure, the game has had its rough times. The Meet Your Match update was an attempt at making TF2 appeal to the e-sports scene, when really it was a game that you could pick up and just... play (hence why Quickplay was a thing). There was (currently remedied) also the botting crisis that lead to all sorts of different things (drama, campaigns, review bombings etc.). None of these affect my opinion on the game itself, however. You don't HAVE to play on Casual and Competitive; you can make your own server or join community ones. I only have minor criticisms with some weapon balancing decisions and bugs, but they aren't enough to lower my thoughts on the game. I do also wish that the classes had more unique lines for interacting with each other, rather than them being stuck to domination lines (think Left 4 Dead 2 or even Overwatch, where characters would refer to each other by name and talk if nearby).

I feel this review was long, long overdue (10 years overdue, even). I never really made serious reviews until now, but I figured I'd finally do so. Team Fortress 2 is not only one of the most important shooters, but also one of the most important games alone to me. It's a game that will never die to me, because even if the official servers shut off, you can still host your own and get others to join or play with singleplayer bots. Even playing with stock weapons is still fun. I'll probably still be playing in a decade or more from now. It just never gets old, even 17 years later.

Team Fortress 2 is a game that I have played since early 2009 (you can check my mercenary badge and achievements if you don't believe me), though my hours don't reflect that for one simple reason: after 2016, trying to play the game for any significant period of time leads to nothing but frustration and tedium. Horribly imbalanced, extremely short matches where the only solution is to wait longer and sit through more loading screens as you queue over and over again hoping for a balanced match.

Before TF2 completely screwed up their official servers, they used to have a server-wide 45 minute time limit that ensured every game mode had a fair chance to be played. Whether you wanted to play Capture the Flag, Attack/Defense, 5CP, KoTH, Payload, or even the other gamemodes, there was a consistency to every match where you knew no matter how good or poorly your team played, you would get to KEEP PLAYING, without interruption.

Speaking of teams playing poorly, there used to be Team Scrambles to help mitigate imbalanced games. These would work without having to interrupt your game with pre-game waiting and server resets. It was simple: if one team won 2 rounds in a row, it would scramble the players around between the two teams at the start of the next round, attempting to create an even points spread. You could also vote for a scramble if it looked hopeless, and there was a cooldown so you couldn't spam scrambles. In Casual, all you can do is requeue and spend even longer waiting and not actually playing or suffer through a 5 minute game.

You could also choose official Valve servers from the server browser, which is how I preferred to find games back then. Instead of waiting, hoping a game with the map you want to play on appears, you could just see for yourself if a map was being played, see its ping and player count, and decide to join it. Now, you are forced to wait in a queue for the game to "graciously allow" you into a server, when there are plenty of open and joinable servers that you would be able to click into in 5 seconds. You can actually see a list of Valve servers online, there are hundreds of them with thousands of players spread throughout them at any moment, but you still have to wait for a game for some reason.

There are other things that Valve removed from official servers too, like the ability to choose your team. You like playing offense more than defense? You could pick BLU when you joined a server, and vice versa. You wanted to duel against your friend? Switch teams. The game is unbalanced and you want to help the losing team? You could. Just the removal of this and the ability to join any server you want means almost every form of player freedom and agency has been removed from official servers since the Meet your Match update of 2016.

I haven't even mentioned yet: half the servers you join into are half-empty. Yes, you will commonly be stuck in a 2v2 or a 3v3 game with no hope of it ever filling up because people cannot find the server and join from the browser or the Quickplay server list, and the matchmaker will not place more people in for whatever reason. The only solution is to requeue and wait even longer, sitting through even more loading screens, just hoping and praying the next game won't be empty as well, and having to wait EVEN! LONGER! if that next game is poor quality.

TF2's anti-cheat (VAC) does legitimately nothing. Blatant or not you will constantly find yourself against cheaters and exploiters in this game. TF2 is very old, and its systems are understood down to a science meaning that cheats and exploits exist for nearly every aspect of this game and on every class in ways that most players simply don't understand. I am a very skilled player, however there is pretty much nothing I can do against cheaters and exploiters other than leaving to find a new match or begging people on the other team (and sometimes my own team) to kick these types of players. The community has done a lot of hard work to report and fix these issues, including giving valve direct code and information on how things happen and how to fix them, yet valve does nothing with it. TF2 dealt with a massive cheating bot issue that lasted multiple years, and during all of this valve was totally fine with releasing more micro-transactions and fixing bugs that only impacted the games economy and income instead of even recognizing the games problemsYour cries for a better anti cheat or to have exploits fixed will never be heard in the games current state.

Casual mode has several issues that make it nearly unplayable for me.
- If you have a high ranking in casual (yes, your casual rank DOES impact the games you get in) You will find yourself constantly in matches that are totally lop-sided. 
- Playing with groups is awful. Casual prioritizes groups in matchmaking however it does not take in consideration group sizes or the overall ranks. Playing with one friend will still put you in servers with 6-stacks of coordinated players while you are put with groups of solo queues that are usually inexperienced.
-  The inclusion of casual to TF2 has killed off being able to play against friends at will. If you want to duel a friend or simply go against them you have to hope that the game auto balances you, or you get lucky and get put into a game against them. There is no way to queue for matches where you can simply be against your group.
- The addition of casual has killed off a majority of the player driven servers and game modes. The funneling nature of casual mode has made turned the once fun discovery of servers into a single action. The average player will stick to casual queue and as a result the once lively community driven server browser is now a ghost town. Many community game modes like Dodgeball, parkour fortress, randomizers, and many others have died out as a result.
- Auto balance is terrible. You can be a top-scoring player and the game will decide to swap you to the other team regardless of your score, time in the server or if you are playing with friends. There have been many instances where i simply stop playing because i am auto-balanced to the losing team moments before the game is won by my previous team. There are many many times where my groups i play with are demotivated to play at all because auto-balance splits us apart mid game or right before the end of a match.

The new player experience is terrible. Valve has put 0 effort into making this game accessible to new users. 
- The in game tutorial does the bare minimum, simply teaching the player about the games movement kit and controls. It does not even cover all of the 9 classes.
- Common quality of life changes like FOV, interp settings, game configurations and performance optimizations are not included in the base game, and require ALOT of external research to figure out. Over the years i have tried to get friends into this game, but often i've come to the conclusion that people aren't interested in setting up and modifying game files and configuration setting to simply play the game comfortably.

Weapons in this game are unbalanced. Weapons can either be meta defining, game-breaking, or totally useless.
- Weapons like the crusaders crossbow are so strong that if players are not running it in matches it is a total hindrance to there team.
- Weapons like the phlog, diamondback, vaccinator and wrangler are so oppressive in matches and they alone can win games if you are running them.
- Weapons like the baby face blaster, ullapool caber and righteous bison have been nerfed so harshly that they might as well not even be in the game. 
These are simply a few examples, but there are significantly more unlocks in this game that are unfun to use or play against.

The economic side of this game is essentially untouchable by the vast majority of the games playerbase. As a long time TF2 trader who has handled many high end items I can say with full confidence that the games economy is not worth interacting with. While I have no issue with free markets the games economic state is very much late stage and cornered.

- Low-end trading is dead. A majority of the low price items within the market have pretty much 0 margin for profit due to the transition of a player to player market, to a cash based one for several reasons weather it be the inclusion of the Steam Community Market, or the rise of automated trade bots taking over third-party trading websites. Low end players will find it easier to just buy with cash rather then interact with a free market and its clear that valve wants this to be the norm with the addition of marketable cosmetics, removal of in-game trade, and discontinuation of old styled crates that promoted trading.

- Valve abuses the player base with FOMO and predatory practices such as releasing seasonal time-limited, cosmetics and unusual effects that incentivise problem spenders, Including gambling in the core gameplay loop by rewarding players with weekly case drops, having game modes that require payment to get cosmetic rewards, and implementing features that keep players spending money such as trade ups, and crafting of hats. Valve will not let you trade newly unboxed items with other players for a week, but they are totally fine with letting you sell it on the Community market instantly, since they get a cut of the sale.

- The economy is currently dealing with hyper-inflation. TF2 has a massive currency issue as well as a cornered high end market. Items received from drops can be used to craft Refined Metal, the games lower end currency. The games economy has to much of this metal, making it very difficult to exchange it for anything of a higher value. When I first started playing this game, Crate keys could be traded for roughly 6 Refined metal. In today's market, you would need to trade 57 Refined metal for a Crate key. Doing anything with Metal is almost always a loss. Valve used to implement things to do with Metal, however ever since Gun Mettle there has been 0 new things you can do with it.

[h1]TF2 Will Never Die Because You Can't Kill Something That Is Already Dead[/h1]

I never thought I'd leave Team Fortress 2 a negative review. Even today, I still believe it's one of the greatest multiplayer shooters ever made. The class design remains nearly unmatched, every mercenary has a distinct personality, the movement is satisfying, the humor is timeless, and its stylized art direction has aged better than most games released a decade later. There is a reason people still return to TF2 after all these years. Unfortunately, there's also a reason I can no longer recommend it, and it has very little to do with the game itself. It has everything to do with Valve.

The biggest example of that neglect was the bot crisis. For years, Casual matchmaking became nearly unplayable as servers filled with aimbots that instantly killed players, blasted music through voice chat, spammed chat endlessly, impersonated well known TF2 creators using AI generated voices, and existed solely to ruin matches. This wasn't a problem hidden from Valve. Everyone knew about it. Players knew, YouTubers knew, and Valve certainly knew, yet almost nothing happened until the #FixTF2 movement generated enough public pressure that ignoring it was no longer an option. Thankfully, the bots are no longer the overwhelming plague they once were, and Valve deserves credit for finally acting. What I can't praise is the fact that it took years of community outrage before one of the most iconic games on Steam received the attention it desperately needed. If Valve was capable of fixing the problem, why did they wait so long?

Unfortunately, removing the bots didn't fix the game. Casual matchmaking is still one of the weakest parts of TF2. Balanced matches feel like the exception rather than the rule, with one team often steamrolling the other within minutes. As players on the losing side inevitably quit, the matchmaking system fills those empty slots by throwing new players into an already hopeless match. You spend more time joining games that are halfway over than actually playing balanced ones. So you leave and search again, only to repeat the exact same process until you eventually give up and close the game. Community servers have become the best way to enjoy Team Fortress 2, but that should never be the answer. Players shouldn't have to avoid Valve's official matchmaking just to experience one of Valve's own games.

What frustrates me even more is Valve's complete lack of direction for TF2. The game doesn't need another Summer update filled with cases. It doesn't need another Smissmas update introducing dozens of new cosmetics, unusual effects, and workshop items that most players will forget about a week later. It needs actual updates. It needs meaningful balance changes, bug fixes, improvements to matchmaking, stronger anti cheat measures, quality of life improvements, and developers willing to maintain one of the greatest multiplayer games ever made. Instead, every seasonal update feels more like another opportunity to sell cosmetic cases than an attempt to improve the game itself. Even the cosmetics have become part of the problem. TF2 built its identity around a consistent visual style where every class had a recognizable silhouette and cosmetics felt like natural extensions of each mercenary. Today, many new additions ignore that identity completely, replacing Valve's carefully crafted art direction with oversized accessories, excessive visual effects, and designs that often look like they belong in an entirely different game.

VAC deserves criticism as well. During the years when TF2 needed it most, Valve's anti cheat system might as well not have existed. Cheaters operated with little fear of punishment while legitimate players slowly lost confidence in the game's official servers. A casual multiplayer game depends on players believing that the developer is protecting the experience. Valve allowed that trust to disappear, and rebuilding it is far more difficult than banning bots after the damage has already been done.

The saddest part is that beneath all of these problems lies one of the best multiplayer games ever created. Every now and then you find a genuinely balanced match where both teams are equally skilled, every class has a purpose, and the game reminds you exactly why people fell in love with it nearly twenty years ago. Those moments still exist, but they feel increasingly rare, and they happen because the community continues to love TF2, not because Valve continues to support it. Community server owners, map creators, artists, modders, and countless passionate players have carried this game for years while Valve has done the bare minimum to keep it standing.

Some people will probably look at the title of this review and point out that TF2 still has tens of thousands of players every day. They're right, but player count isn't what I'm talking about. A game isn't alive simply because people are still playing it. It's alive when its developers continue to improve it, support it, and give players reasons to believe its future matters. Valve stopped treating Team Fortress 2 like an active game years ago. Today, meaningful updates have been replaced by cosmetic cases, official matchmaking is still frustrating, and basic maintenance is celebrated as though it were a major expansion because expectations have become so low.

That's why I say TF2 is already dead. Not because the players abandoned it, but because its creators did. The only reason it continues to exist is because one of the most passionate communities in gaming refuses to let it disappear. TF2 will never truly die, because you can't kill something that is already dead.
